2.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what do you ask a shoulder patient?"
- "Pain, instability, stiffness, weakness, swelling, clicking and deformity."
- "Age, dominant hand, job and sport come first."
- "Then neck symptoms, trauma, previous dislocations and operations."

### Age points to the disease
| Age | Think of |
|---|---|
| Young | instability |
| Middle age | impingement |
| Older | rotator cuff tear, arthritis |

- **Memory:** young slips, middle pinches, old tears

### Pain — where and when
| Pain | Think of |
|---|---|
| Over the deltoid, not past the elbow | shoulder joint or cuff |
| One finger on the ACJ | acromioclavicular joint (ACJ) |
| Neck to scapula, tingling to the hand | cervical spine |
| At the deltoid insertion, mid-arm | glenohumeral arthritis |

| Timing (Nagah) | Think of |
|---|---|
| Mid-arc of elevation | cuff, subacromial impingement |
| Last degrees of elevation | ACJ |
| During throwing | SLAP lesion (superior labrum anterior to posterior) |
| At night | cuff, frozen shoulder, arthritis; infection or tumour |

- Night pain is common here; alone it is not a red flag
- Severe pain, negative tests → acute calcific tendinitis or early frozen shoulder

### Instability, stiffness, weakness
#### Instability — four questions (Nagah)
| Ask | Why |
|---|---|
| How many dislocations? | recurrence |
| When was the last one? | activity |
| Reduced by self, doctor, anaesthesia? | severity |
| Epilepsy? | posterior dislocation; fits cause recurrence |

- Ask: "Can you put it out on purpose?" (voluntary)
- **Memory:** TUBS = traumatic, unidirectional, Bankart, surgery; AMBRI = atraumatic, multidirectional, bilateral, rehabilitation, inferior shift

#### Stiffness and weakness
- Stiff = active and passive both lost; weak with no pain → cuff tear or nerve

#### Ask every time
| Complaint | Ask |
|---|---|
| Pain | site, onset, night, relation to the arc |
| Function | hair, back pocket, overhead, sport |
| Past | trauma, neck, diabetes, cancer, breast surgery |

- **Red flags:** weight loss, fever, previous malignancy → infection or tumour
- **Memory:** seven complaints — pain, instability, stiffness, swelling, weakness, clicking, deformity
- General history and opening → ch 1

2.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "examine this shoulder"
- "Standing, undressed to the waist: look front, side, back and axilla."
- "Feel from the SCJ to the scapular spine; then move, active then passive."
- "Power of the cuff, special tests, instability sitting or supine; neck and neuro last."

- **Whole shoulder exam (video):** [▶ Dr James Gill · 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DpBiXTVNadA)

### The route on one page
| Position | What you do (in order) |
|---|---|
| Standing | Look: front, side, back, axilla |
| Standing | Neck screen: does neck movement bring the pain? |
| Standing | Feel: SCJ, clavicle, ACJ, coracoid, GT, groove, spine |
| Standing | Move: active then passive; rhythm, arc, Apley |
| Standing | Power: cuff, then deltoid, trapezius, serratus |
| Standing | Special: impingement, cuff, biceps/SLAP, ACJ |
| Sitting or supine | Instability: sulcus, drawer, apprehension, relocation |
| Finish | Neuro C5–T1, axillary nerve, pulses, neck (Spurling) |

- GT = greater tuberosity; ER / IR = external / internal rotation; SCJ = sternoclavicular joint
- **Memory:** Look, Feel, Move, Measure (power), Special (instability), Neuro, Vascular, Joints above/below

### Standing — Look
#### Look — front, side, back, axilla
- Expose to the waist, scapulae visible; watch undressing

| View | Look for |
|---|---|
| Front | levels, contour, deltoid, SCJ, clavicle, ACJ |
| Side | squared shoulder, prominent acromion, deltoid bulk |
| Back | scapula height, winging, fossae, trapezius |
| Axilla | scars, nodes, neurofibroma patches |

[[FIG: Fig 2.1 — Inspection: front, side, behind, axilla · 2.02

#### Wasting and contour
| Sign | Means |
|---|---|
| Hollow above the scapular spine | supraspinatus: cuff tear or suprascapular nerve |
| Hollow below the spine | infraspinatus: cuff tear or spinoglenoid notch |
| Flat deltoid, squared shoulder | axillary nerve palsy or anterior dislocation |
| Drooping shoulder, thin trapezius | spinal accessory nerve (node biopsy) |

[[FIG: Fig 2.2 — Trapezius wasting; supraspinatus and infraspinatus wasting · 2.02

#### Deformity
| Sign | Means |
|---|---|
| **Popeye** bulge low on the arm | ruptured long head of biceps |
| Lost anterior axillary fold | pectoralis major rupture |
| Prominent ACJ or SCJ | dislocation or arthritis |
| Step in the clavicle | old fracture or non-union |
| High small scapula | Sprengel's shoulder |

[[FIG: Fig 2.3 — Popeye sign: biceps belly drops after long head rupture · 2.02
[[FIG: Fig 2.4 — Prominent ACJ and SCJ · 2.02

#### Winging
| Winging | Muscle | Nerve |
|---|---|---|
| Medial (border lifts) | serratus anterior | long thoracic (C5–7) |
| Lateral (angle swings out) | trapezius | spinal accessory |

- **Memory:** serratus → medial; trapezius → lateral (Nagah)
- Pain alone can cause subtle dynamic winging

[[FIG: Fig 2.5 — Medial winging from serratus palsy · 2.02

### Standing — Feel
- Stand behind the seated patient; watch the face in a mirror

| Order | Landmark | Tender means |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | SCJ, 2 cm lateral to the sternal notch | injury, infection, arthritis |
| 2 | Clavicle | fracture, non-union |
| 3 | ACJ | ACJ arthritis or injury |
| 4 | Coracoid, 2 cm below the clavicle's lateral–middle third junction | frozen shoulder, pectoralis minor |
| 5 | GT, anterior and lateral acromion | cuff, subacromial bursa |
| 6 | Bicipital groove, arm in 10° IR | biceps tendinitis |
| 7 | Scapular spine, fossae | wasting, scapular lesion |

- **Memory:** "SCJ to ACJ, coracoid, then GT and groove, then the back"

[[FIG: Fig 2.6 — Palpation from the SCJ outward; biceps groove · 2.02

### Standing — Move
#### Active, then passive
- Watch abduction from the front and from behind

| Movement (Nagah) | Normal |
|---|---|
| Forward flexion | 160–180° |
| Abduction | 160–180° |
| Extension | 50–60° |
| External rotation, elbow at side | 45–90° |
| Internal rotation, thumb up the back | T7–T9 |
| Adduction | hand over the opposite shoulder |

- Flexion of 180° is usually a trick: the patient leans back

[[FIG: Fig 2.7 — Forward flexion and extension · 2.02
[[FIG: Fig 2.8 — ER at the side, active and passive · 2.02
[[FIG: Fig 2.9 — IR: thumb up the back, level noted · 2.02

#### Scapulohumeral rhythm
- Glenohumeral to scapulothoracic movement = **2:1** (Exam Techniques)
- Fix the scapula → abduction stops near 80° in neutral rotation (Exam Techniques)

| Abnormal rhythm | Means |
|---|---|
| Early shrug, scapula leads | cuff tear, arthritis, stiff joint |
| Cannot start abduction | massive cuff tear or deltoid palsy (Nagah) |

[[FIG: Fig 2.10 — Abduction from behind; scapula fixed · 2.02

#### Apley scratch test
- Over the head to the opposite scapula = abduction, ER
- Behind the back to the opposite scapula = adduction, IR; note the level

[[FIG: Fig 2.11 — Apley scratch: over and behind · 2.02

### Standing — Power
- Cuff as a group first, then the girdle; cuff table and lag signs → 2.3

| Muscle | Test | Nerve |
|---|---|---|
| Deltoid | resisted flexion, abduction, extension | axillary C5–6 |
| Trapezius | shrug against resistance | spinal accessory |
| Serratus anterior | wall push-up; watch the scapula | long thoracic |
| Rhomboids | hands on hips, push elbows back | dorsal scapular C5 |
| Latissimus dorsi | pull the elbow down | thoracodorsal C6–8 |
| Pectoralis major | hands on hips, squeeze in | medial and lateral pectoral |

- **Memory:** front: deltoid, pectoralis, latissimus; back: trapezius, rhomboids, serratus

[[FIG: Fig 2.12 — Deltoid, trapezius and pectoralis against resistance · 2.02

### Finish
- Neuro C5–T1 → ch 9; axillary nerve, plexus → ch 5, ch 6
- Pulses: radial, brachial; neck: Spurling's test

[[FIG: Fig 2.13 — Axillary nerve: sensation over the lateral deltoid · 2.02

PITFALL — "forcing the apprehension position"
- The test can dislocate an unstable shoulder
- Say → "**I stop at the first sign of apprehension; I do not need to dislocate it.**"

2.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "is the cuff torn or is the shoulder stiff?"
- "Active lost, passive full → cuff tear or nerve palsy."
- "Active and passive both lost → frozen shoulder or arthritis; the X-ray separates them."

### Cuff muscle by muscle
| Muscle | Power test | Lag or sign | Nerve |
|---|---|---|---|
| Supraspinatus | Jobe (empty can) | drop arm | suprascapular C5–6 |
| Infraspinatus | resisted ER, elbow at side | ER lag sign | suprascapular C5–6 |
| Teres minor | resisted ER in 90° abduction | hornblower | axillary C5–6 |
| Subscapularis | lift-off, belly press, bear hug | IR lag sign | upper and lower subscapular |

- **Memory:** one power test and one lag test for each of the four (Prof Rashwan)
- Subscapularis tests: compare sides, or the tear is missed

[[FIG: Fig 2.14 — Resisted ER and IR with the elbow at the side · 2.03

### Active versus passive range
- Passive lost too → mechanical block: frozen shoulder, arthritis, locked dislocation (Prof Rashwan)

### Frozen shoulder, arthritis or cuff tear?
| | Frozen shoulder | Glenohumeral osteoarthritis (OA) | Cuff tear |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active range | lost, all planes | lost | lost |
| Passive range | lost, all planes | lost | full |
| ER | lost most | lost | weak, not stiff |
| Crepitus | no | yes | sometimes |
| X-ray | normal | joint narrowing, osteophytes | high head in old tears |

- Loss of passive ER = the key sign of frozen shoulder and OA
- Diabetes → frozen shoulder more common, worse and longer

[[FIG: Fig 2.15 — Passive ER at the side: lost in frozen shoulder · 2.03

PITFALL — "which rotation goes first in frozen shoulder?"
- Books differ: ER lost most (capsular pattern) or IR lost first
- Say → "**Frozen shoulder loses movement in all planes; passive ER loss is the sign I show.**"

2.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which tests for which question?"
- "Impingement: Neer, Hawkins. Cuff: one test per muscle. Biceps: Speed, Yergason."
- "SLAP: O'Brien, crank. ACJ: cross-body. Instability: apprehension, relocation, sulcus, drawer."

### Is the cuff impinging?
#### Neer impingement sign
- **Aim:** subacromial impingement
- **How:** fix the scapula; lift the internally rotated arm passively
- **Positive:** pain as the arm rises → impingement
- **Why:** GT and cuff hit the anterior acromion
- **Trap:** Neer *test* = pain gone after subacromial local anaesthetic
- **Video:** [▶ AMBOSS · 1:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g92VbV56AAY)

[[FIG: Fig 2.16 — Neer sign: passive elevation, scapula fixed · 2.04

#### Hawkins–Kennedy test
- **Aim:** subacromial impingement
- **How:** arm and elbow at 90° flexion; you internally rotate the arm
- **Positive:** pain → impingement or cuff disease
- **Why:** GT and cuff rotate under the coracoacromial ligament
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8kSXeXFGuME)

[[FIG: Fig 2.17 — Hawkins–Kennedy: internal rotation at 90° flexion · 2.04

#### Painful arc
- **Aim:** where the pain sits in the arc
- **How:** patient abducts slowly to full elevation
- **Positive:** pain 60–120° → cuff or impingement; last degrees → ACJ (Nagah)
- **Why:** cuff passes under the acromion mid-arc
- **Video:** [▶ AMBOSS · 2:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zMnjj7YV-40)

[[FIG: Fig 2.18 — Painful arc of abduction · 2.04

### Is the cuff torn?
#### Jobe (empty can) test
- **Aim:** supraspinatus
- **How:** arm 90° abducted, scapular plane, thumb down; you push down
- **Positive:** pain → tendinopathy; weakness → tear
- **Why:** full IR takes the deltoid out
- **Trap:** full can (thumb up) hurts less, equally accurate (Exam Techniques)
- **Video:** [▶ AMBOSS · 1:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXYN9bnu0C0)

[[FIG: Fig 2.19 — Jobe test: scapular plane, thumb down · 2.04

#### Drop arm test
- **Aim:** large supraspinatus tear
- **How:** abduct the arm fully; patient lowers it slowly
- **Positive:** arm drops suddenly near shoulder level → large tear (Reider)
- **Why:** no cuff to control the lowering
- **Trap:** axillary nerve palsy gives the same sign
- **Video:** [▶ Mike Reinold · 0:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LhRiEvdZZkg)

[[FIG: Fig 2.20 — Drop arm: lowered part-way, then falls · 2.04

#### External rotation lag sign
- **Aim:** infraspinatus tear
- **How:** elbow 90° at the side; rotate fully out, let go
- **Positive:** forearm drifts back to neutral → infraspinatus tear
- **Why:** no active ER to hold the position
- **Trap:** suprascapular nerve palsy gives the same lag
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iUTxEAOrEMY)

[[FIG: Fig 2.21 — ER lag: held, then drifts in · 2.04

#### Hornblower sign
- **Aim:** teres minor
- **How:** arm and elbow at 90°; patient holds ER
- **Positive:** arm falls into IR → teres minor tear
- **Why:** teres minor is the main ER in abduction
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RQakGuCRJ0E)

[[FIG: Fig 2.22 — Hornblower: normal, then abnormal · 2.04

#### Gerber lift-off test
- **Aim:** subscapularis
- **How:** back of hand on the lumbar spine; patient lifts off
- **Positive:** cannot lift off → subscapularis tear
- **Why:** hand behind the back cuts out pectoralis
- **Trap:** needs full IR; stiff shoulders cannot do it
- **Video:** [▶ AMBOSS · 1:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t9dSDVRbjn0)

[[FIG: Fig 2.23 — Lift-off: hand pushed away from the back · 2.04

#### Belly press (Napoleon) test
- **Aim:** subscapularis when IR is lost
- **How:** hand pressed on the abdomen, elbow kept forward
- **Positive:** elbow drops back, wrist flexes → subscapularis
- **Why:** elbow forward needs subscapularis, not pectoralis
- **Video:** [▶ AMBOSS · 2:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q2_HcOlgfZM)

[[FIG: Fig 2.24 — Belly press: elbow forward is normal · 2.04

#### Bear hug test
- **Aim:** subscapularis, upper part
- **How:** palm on the opposite shoulder; you try to lift it off
- **Positive:** hand lifts off → subscapularis tear
- **Why:** resisted IR in flexion isolates subscapularis
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3psqKDWK0o4)

[[FIG: Fig 2.25 — Bear hug: hand held on the opposite shoulder · 2.04

### Is the biceps or labrum the cause?
#### Speed test
- **Aim:** long head of biceps
- **How:** arm 90° flexed, elbow straight, palm up; you push down
- **Positive:** pain in the bicipital groove → biceps tendinitis
- **Why:** loads the long head over the shoulder
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6rzi_zBYJNU)

[[FIG: Fig 2.26 — Speed test: resisted flexion, palm up · 2.04

#### Yergason test
- **Aim:** long head of biceps
- **How:** elbow 90° at the side, pronated; patient supinates against you
- **Positive:** groove pain → tendinitis; pop → unstable tendon (Nagah)
- **Why:** biceps = main supinator with the elbow flexed
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JMKwNRLHIvY)

[[FIG: Fig 2.27 — Yergason test: resisted supination · 2.04

#### O'Brien (active compression) test
- **Aim:** SLAP lesion or ACJ
- **How:** arm 90° flexed, 10–15° adducted, thumb down; resist; repeat palm up
- **Positive:** pain thumb down, eased palm up; deep → SLAP (Reider)
- **Why:** thumb down loads the labrum and the ACJ
- **Video:** [▶ The Physio Channel · 1:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=brc8UPT218M)

[[FIG: Fig 2.28 — O'Brien: thumb down, then palm up · 2.04

#### Crank test
- **Aim:** labral tear
- **How:** arm 120° abducted; axial load, rotate in and out (Nagah)
- **Positive:** pain or click → labral tear
- **Why:** the head grinds the torn labrum

### Is the ACJ the cause?
#### Cross-body adduction (scarf) test
- **Aim:** ACJ pain
- **How:** arm at shoulder height; push it across the chest
- **Positive:** ACJ pain → arthritis or injury
- **Why:** adduction compresses the ACJ
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yfZFbnbsOCo)

[[FIG: Fig 2.30 — Scarf test: elbow pushed across the chest · 2.04

### Is the shoulder unstable?
- **Memory:** laxity tests measure; provocative tests reproduce the fear (Reider)
- Generalised laxity → Beighton score → ch 1

#### Apprehension test
- **Aim:** anterior instability
- **How:** supine, couch edge; arm and elbow at 90°; rotate out
- **Positive:** fear, guarding → anterior instability
- **Why:** abduction and ER = the position of dislocation
- **Trap:** pain without fear → internal impingement (Reider)
- **Video:** [▶ UW Family Medicine · 0:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qKqJRrms4u8)

[[FIG: Fig 2.31 — Anterior apprehension, sitting and supine · 2.04

#### Relocation (Jobe) test
- **Aim:** confirm anterior instability
- **How:** in apprehension position, push the head backward
- **Positive:** fear goes; let go suddenly → fear returns (release test)
- **Why:** the push holds the head in the socket
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 1:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kthWchPH6iE)

[[FIG: Fig 2.32 — Relocation, then release · 2.04

#### Anterior and posterior drawer test (shoulder)
- **Aim:** anterior and posterior laxity
- **How:** stand behind; fix the scapula; shift the head forward and back
- **Positive:** more than the sound side → laxity in that direction
- **Why:** normal head moves about 25% forward, 50% back (Reider)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotherapy UC Copenhagen · 0:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G8s_7Q5zfTM)

[[FIG: Fig 2.33 — Drawer: scapula fixed, head shifted · 2.04

#### Load and shift test
- **Aim:** grade the laxity
- **How:** load the head into the glenoid, then shift it
- **Positive:** grade 1 = 25–50%; 2 = 50–100%; 3 = dislocates (Hawkins)
- **Why:** loading centres the head, so the shift is measured
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 2:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=txARar71h5E)

[[FIG: Fig 2.34 — Load and shift, sitting and supine · 2.04

#### Sulcus sign
- **Aim:** inferior laxity
- **How:** sitting, arm relaxed; pull the arm down
- **Positive:** gap under the acromion → inferior laxity; graded 1–3 (Nagah)
- **Why:** head slides down out of the glenoid
- **Trap:** still present in ER → rotator interval lax
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vV7u2JtdYWI)

[[FIG: Fig 2.35 — Sulcus under the acromion on downward pull · 2.04

#### Posterior apprehension test
- **Aim:** posterior instability
- **How:** arm 90° flexed, adducted, in IR; push back along the humerus
- **Positive:** pain or guarding → posterior instability
- **Why:** pushes the head out the back
- **Video:** [▶ The Physio Channel · 0:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CHzJk5IeCkk)

[[FIG: Fig 2.36 — Posterior apprehension: flexion, adduction, axial load · 2.04

#### Jerk test
- **Aim:** posterior instability, posterior labrum
- **How:** arm 90° abducted, in IR; axial load into adduction (Nagah)
- **Positive:** pain or a clunk → posterior instability
- **Why:** head jerks out the back, then in
- **Video:** [▶ Stanford Medicine 25 · 1:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kjGmQneky5w)

#### Neer impingement sign

- **How:** fix the scapula; lift the internally rotated arm passively
- **Positive:** pain as the arm rises → impingement

#### Hawkins–Kennedy test
- **Aim:** subacromial impingement
- **How:** arm and elbow at 90° flexion; you internally rotate the arm
- **Positive:** pain → impingement or cuff disease
- **Why:** GT and cuff rotate under the coracoacromial ligament
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho Eval Pal (Paul Marquis PT) · 0:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8kSXeXFGuME)

[[FIG: Fig 2.17 — Hawkins–Kennedy: internal rotation at 90° flexion · 2.04

#### Painful arc
- **Aim:** where the pain sits in the arc
- **How:** patient abducts slowly to full elevation
- **Positive:** pain 60–120° → cuff or impingement; last degrees → ACJ (Nagah)
- **Why:** cuff passes under the acromion mid-arc
- **Video:** [▶ AMBOSS · 2:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zMnjj7YV-40)

[[FIG: Fig 2.18 — Painful arc of abduction · 2.04

2.04.2.b:
#### Jobe (empty can) test
- **Aim:** supraspinatus
- **How:** arm 90° abducted, scapular plane, thumb down; you push down
- **Positive:** pain → tendinopathy; weakness → tear
- **Why:** full IR takes the deltoid out
- **Trap:** full can (thumb up) hurts less, equally accurate (Exam Techniques)
- **Video:** [▶ AMBOSS · 1:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXYN9bnu0C0)

#### Drop arm test
- **Aim:** large supraspinatus tear
- **How:** abduct the arm fully; patient lowers it slowly
- **Positive:** arm drops suddenly near shoulder level → large tear (Reider)
- **Why:** no cuff to control the lowering
- **Trap:** axillary nerve palsy gives the same sign
- **Video:** [▶ Mike Reinold · 0:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LhRiEvdZZkg)

[[FIG: Fig 2.20 — Drop arm: lowered part-way, then falls · 2.04

- **Aim:** infraspinatus tear
- **How:** elbow 90° at the side; rotate fully out, let go
- **Positive:** forearm drifts back to neutral → infraspinatus tear
- **Why:** no active ER to hold the position
- **Trap:** suprascapular nerve palsy gives the same lag
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iUTxEAOrEMY)

- **Aim:** teres minor
- **How:** arm and elbow at 90°; patient holds ER
- **Positive:** arm falls into IR → teres minor tear
- **Why:** teres minor is the main ER in abduction

- "Who, dominant hand, job; main complaint; standing findings; range; cuff; special tests."

### Present it like this (model cuff-tear case)
| Part | Say |
|---|---|
| History | "A 62-year-old right-handed builder; right shoulder pain and weakness, 1 year." |
| Look | "Wasting of supraspinatus and infraspinatus; no winging." |
| Move | "Active elevation 90°, passive full; painful arc." |
| Power | "Jobe weak, ER lag positive; subscapularis intact." |
| Verdict | "Posterosuperior cuff tear; I would request ultrasound or MRI." |

### Differential of a painful shoulder
| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| Subacromial | impingement, cuff tear, calcific tendinitis |
| Joint | frozen shoulder, OA, rheumatoid, infection |
| ACJ | arthritis, injury |
| Unstable | anterior, posterior, multidirectional |
| Referred | neck, brachial neuritis, heart, gallbladder |

- **Memory:** "SAJ-UR" — subacromial, ACJ, joint, unstable, referred

| Active lost, passive full? | cuff tear or nerve palsy |

| Subscapularis behind the back — why? | removes pectoralis major |
| Teres minor test? | hornblower sign |
